body_markdown:
Cast your mind back to 1996. The Bayside Boys remix of “Macarena” is all the rage, the dot-com bubble is inflating at a terrifying rate, and a pint of lager still leaves change from a fiver.


In the automotive world, the roadster is undergoing a renaissance. The[Mazda Miata](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mazda/mx~5_miata/1991/1991-mazda-mx~5_miata-base?id=aCn1I000000DREPSA4) has successfully proven that the British sports car concept works brilliantly when assembled by people who understand waterproofing. BMW is flogging the[Z3](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=bmw+z3) on the back of Pierce Brosnan’s James Bond, and Porsche is betting the entire farm on the mid-engined[Boxster](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/porsche/boxster/1997/1997-porsche-boxster-base?id=aCn1I000000CxH4SAK) .


And then, into this fray, strolls Mercedes-Benz. Not with a traditional ragtop, nor a stripped-out track weapon, but with a technological party trick that rewrites the rulebook.


Mercedes-Benz AG


The R170 SLK—short for *Sportlich, Leicht, und Kurz* (Sporty, Light, and Short)—didn’t just move the goalposts; it folded them up, packed them into the trunk, and drove off. The Vario Roof was a stroke of absolute genius. At the push of a button, an intricate ballet of hydraulic rams and folding metal transformed a snug, refined winter coupe into a sun-drenched roadster in just 25 seconds. Peugeot had experimented with the idea decades earlier with the Eclipse, as had Ford with its Skyliner, but Stuttgart perfected it. Overnight, the canvas roof felt utterly archaic.


Mercedes-Benz AG


Mercedes-Benz AG


Yet, for all its structural brilliance, the R170 Mercedes-Benz SLK has spent the better part of two decades fighting a frankly tedious image problem. Slapped with the lazy “hairdresser’s car” moniker by pub bores whose driving experience rarely extended beyond an Olds Achieva, the SLK was dismissed by purists as a boulevard cruiser. But view the R170 through the lens of a modern classic, and you quickly realize those critics were missing the point entirely.


Approach an early SLK today, and the[Bruno Sacco-directed](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/bruno-saccos-designs-took-mercedes-benz-to-new-heights/) styling has aged remarkably well. There is a chunky, carved-from-solid aesthetic to the R170 that later, more bulbous Mercedes designs lost. The twin power bulges on the hood are a delightful, unapologetic nod to the legendary[300SL Gullwing](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mercedes-benz/300sl) , while the truncated rear end gives it a purposeful, wedgy stance. Inside, Mercedes went remarkably bold for a company usually associated with somber charcoal cabins. You could spec your SLK with two-tone leather in vibrant scarlet or lurid yellow, offset by faux carbon fiber trim that screamed late-’90s optimism. It feels surprisingly intimate, but the ergonomics are pure, uncorrupted Mercedes: logical, robust, and built for immense mileage.


Mercedes-Benz AG


Turn the key, however, and the initial aural experience is somewhat at odds with the elegant exterior. The defining engine of the pre-2000 era is the SLK 230 Kompressor. Under the hood lies the M111 2.3-liter four-cylinder engine, a unit that owes more to Stuttgart’s taxi heritage than its motorsport division. At idle, it is undeniably gruff. It clatters with a utilitarian, industrial rhythm that entirely lacks the cultured, mechanical thrum of a Porsche flat-six or the silky hum of a BMW straight-six.


But pull the chunky gear selector into Drive—because here you really do want the slick five-speed automatic over the notoriously notchy manual—pin the throttle, and all is forgiven. As the revs climb, the gruffness is drowned out by the distinct, industrial whine of the Eaton M62 supercharger. It sounds like a miniature jet turbine spooling up, and it delivers a thick, meaty wodge of mid-range torque. With 192 horsepower and 206 lb-ft of twist available from just 2500 rpm, the 230 Kompressor doesn’t need to be wrung by its neck. It surges forward on a relentless wave of forced induction, dispatching overtakes with a muscular, effortless shove that feels wonderfully old school.


Mercedes-Benz AG


Throw it into a series of demanding back road bends, and the SLK’s true character reveals itself. If you approach it expecting the scalpel-sharp turn-in and mid-corner adjustability of a Boxster, you will walk away disappointed. The R170 utilizes a a relatively slow, lightly assisted rack-and-pinion setup. It results in a helm that is undeniably vague off-center, requiring a moment to translate your inputs to the front wheels.


But to criticize the SLK for not being a Boxster is to criticize a hammer for not being a scalpel. The SLK is not a pure sports car in the Boxster sense; it is a small-scale grand tourer. Treat it as a pocket-sized SL and it suddenly makes perfect sense. The ride, while firm over urban ridges, settles into a glorious, long-legged lope at highway speeds. The chassis is astonishingly stiff with the roof up, banishing the scuttle-shake that plagued its contemporaries. You pilot the SLK with your fingertips, riding that supercharged torque curve, pointing the long hood toward the horizon and letting the car’s inherent waft-ability do the heavy lifting. Here is a car designed to cover hundreds of miles at a time and still leave you feeling fresh enough to order a martini at the other end.


Mercedes-Benz AG


Mercedes-Benz AG


Mercedes-Benz AG


If you desire a sweeter soundtrack there’s the post-2000 facelift introduced the SLK 320, which packs 215 horses from its buttery-smooth M112 3.2-liter V-6. It lacks the punchy, low-down urgency of the Kompressor, but it transforms the car into a genuinely luxurious prospect, complete with upgraded interior materials and standard ESP to rein in the occasionally lively rear axle in the wet. Cars equipped with manual transmissions also gained an extra gear. In 2001, AMG contributed its own version; the resulting SLK 32 AMG packs 349 hp.


The R170 was replaced by the R171 SLK in 2004, but as this era fell within the DaimerChrysler marriage, car spotters will note that the bones of the R170 (80% of them, in fact) lived on for a further four years in the Chrysler Crossfire.


Over the last decade, #1 (concours)[values for SLK 230s](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mercedes~benz/slk_230/2001/2001-mercedes~benz-slk_230-base?id=aCn1I000000DSSKSA4) and[320s are up](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mercedes~benz/slk320/2001/2001-mercedes~benz-slk320-base?id=aCn1I000000Cwu8SAC) 39% and 33%, respectively. Prices peaked from mid-2022 to mid-2024, with #1 values for both models topping out at just over $26,000. Over the last two years, both have dropped roughly 15%–20% from those highs. Unsurprisingly, buyers tend to favor the refinement and extra power of the SLK 320, and it carries a slight premium over the SLK 230—roughly $1000–$3000 depending on condition. If a concours example isn’t in the budget, it’s not hard to find solid drivers in #3 (good) condition for less than ten grand.


Mercedes-Benz AG


Of course, buying an R170 today requires going in eyes wide open. One of the biggest issues is rust. This era of Mercedes-Benz was infamously plagued by cost-cutting and a switch to water-based paints, meaning SLKs can dissolve with terrifying enthusiasm. Front fenders, rear wheel arches, the trunk lock surround, and the spring perches must be inspected with clinical paranoia. Mechanically, these Benzes are largely strong, but you should check the K40 relay module—the unit that sends power to various electrical components and control modules. These are notorious for dry solder joints that cause intermittent starting issues. It is crucial to ensure the complex roof mechanism operates smoothly and without leaks. And interior soft-touch plastics have a habit of peeling away like bad sunburn.


Find a good one, however, and the Mercedes-Benz R170 SLK represents one of the most compelling modern classic bargains currently on the market. It is a car that democratized the folding hardtop, wrapping strong mechanicals and genuinely punchy performance in a shell that still garners admiring glances.


It is time to ditch the outdated clichés and view the R170 for what it truly is: a brilliantly engineered, all-weather cruiser with a heavy-hitting supercharged punch. It’s Stuttgart’s miniature grand tourer, and it is finally coming of age.


Mercedes-Benz AG
